en: I heard he sought a hero.
To satisfy his longing beyond measure,
I heard he sought a lion.
If we ride farther from here,
There lies that yellow, hilly ridge.
Azhybay, born a leader,
Is the hero we should welcome.
If you welcome the hero Azhy,
He will be a man of surpassing spiritual might,
He will be khan to the forty champions.
His tales will console a soul,
His deeds will gladden a soul.
His laughter will bring out the sun;
The mortal who welcomes him will rejoice.
He is the keen one and the support.
If Azhybay falls into your hands,
He is the hero to keep without letting go.
When you meet, he will settle the proper course.
Until your worthy life has passed,
He will remain your companion.
He is your shelter and your support;
He is a people who will care for you.
The finest son of Argyn Khan,
They named him Azhybay.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay
Does not come to just any mortal.
My champion whom Kydyr has blessed,
Except for you, blessed by Kydyr,
That Azhybay will be found by no one.
Sharing death, united in life,
Such is Azhybay's nature.
He is the champion and the support,
He is the hero to bind about your waist.
Entering battle, a destroyer;
Resting in camp, a maker of laughter.
In peacetime, a sharer in acquired wealth,
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
If you die, your companion in faith.
Your Azhy, whose ways are different,
Which of his cares shall I recount?
In battle, a companion with the spear;
On a raid, a companion in the gains.
Azhybay, full of wisdom,
Is a skilled servant, nimble with a spear.
If trouble falls upon your apple-like head,
He is a mighty servant who will bring you out.
He is your prop and your support.
When bullets pour down like rain,
When strife erupts and a troublemaker rises,
Beneath the banner, without flinching,
He is the hero who will stand firm.
Traveling farther from here,
Let us search this way and that.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
If Allah Most High decrees,
Let us find Azhybay.
Wolf-maned hero Azhybay,
Let us send him as an envoy.
Whether they will give it or refuse,
Let us hear from Azhybay.
If they will not heed our words,
If they will not give Akkelte,
Let us go out to a place of battle.
If they will not give Akkelte,
Let us exchange much gunfire.
Let us turn our horses' heads,
Let us wage war for six days.
Let us exchange much gunfire,
Let us seize Akkelte back!’
Thus speaking, hero Bakay
Rose and said his prayers.
They saddled their wondrous steeds.
The bloodthirsty heroes steeled themselves,
Wrathful, making ready,
Girding on swords without scabbards,
Taking weapons, preparing themselves.
To your elder, leopard Bakay,
Wisdom came from the unseen.
Over his chest, impervious to bullets,
In armor half an armspan long,
Your wolf-maned hero rode exultant,
Into the struggle to take Akkelte.
Your elder Bakay, his companion,
Of bloodthirsty, wolf-maned Manas,
Was the confidant for the other world.
Riding a horse like the gray wondrous steed,
Wolf-maned Bakay the saint,
Who knew things from afar,
Your elder Bakay the sage,
Together with generous Manas,
Churning their powdery trail into dust,
Their two mountain-sized steeds,
They galloped on without a halt.
Crossing ridge after hilly ridge,
The rough, mottled hillocks
They left behind as they went.
Ahead of the lion hero,
Your wolf-maned lion Bakay,
Along many and varied roads,
Went leading the way.
The wondrous steeds beneath them,
Water flowed from their flanks,
Steam issued from their nostrils,
The ground they trod crumbled to dust.
Their breath issuing from their nostrils
Billowed like a hide-smoking pit.
They rode them on at a lofty stride,
Trotting them with a jolting gait.
With no mountain the size of a knucklebone,
No hollow the size of a saddlecloth,
Into the deserted dark plain
They now entered.
The wondrous steeds, exceptionally swift,
Gouged the ground where they stepped.
The white reins, round-braided,
Stretched tight in their palms.
They made them prance and surge,
Tossing as though their husbands had died.
Racing against flying birds,
The white lead ropes, thick as wrists,
Were clenched tight in their hands.
The tireless wondrous steeds,
Their hooves clattered on the ground;
The bits of black steel
Clanged within their throats.
The ground they trod crumbled to dust.
All their coat-tails and sleeves
Flapped behind them.
Crossing a rugged, narrow pass,
Traversing uneven ground,
How could the noble ones spare themselves?
They drew near Ak-Talaa.
To the point where the desert ended,
To a jutting promontory,
They had just arrived.
Crossing the winding desert,
Fording crooked, twisting waters,
Their coats of mail flashing,
The sweat flowing from their flanks
Splashed against the stirrups.
They traveled no little distance;
They went far, not sparing their horses.
Dawn broke, swelling into sight,
Dawn shone white and vast,
Dawn rose and parted,
Light poured upon the earth.
The reed-tops rattled,
Young larks chirped,
Mist lifted from the ground.
Then the face of the world
Appeared as bright as glass.
If you looked at what came into view,
He rode a horse like Kartküröng,
And wore a black, bulletproof coat.
Making the Brown horse prance,
He had tied its horsehair tail tight.
Through fescue and forage kochia,
He had worn his horse's hocks,
Over all the world
He had wandered in hardship.
Forked beard, ruddy face,
Towering in stature, broad in the shoulders,
Broad across, with a camel calf's eyes,
A clear, fine form, sweet words,
Broad shoulders befitting a hero,
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
It was Azhybay himself.
Not only your Azhy himself,
But his own dark, gazing eyes.
Scouting and viewing the land,
He had gone out hunting.
Pursuing wild asses in the desert,
Into a great, unending
Turmoil he had entered.
He had crossed ruined Chambyl,
And without turning aside, Bukhara's
Eastern side he had traversed.
Chasing antelope from sharp stubble,
He had felled them where they grew exhausted.
Chasing wild asses in the desert,
He had caught them by whole herds.
Stalking mountain sheep, pursuing wild asses,
He had plunged into the hunt.
Satisfying his longing to the death,
He had plunged into the dust.
Where no child of man traveled,
To such a place he had come.
Where no winged bird could fly,
To such a desert he had come.
You will have heard of it:
Azhybay's Brown horse,
Sparse of tail and scant of mane,
Let no wild ass escape its pursuit.
He had hunted wild asses and slaughtered them.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay
Some forty wild asses
Had gathered on the plain.
The Brown horse, big as a dromedary,
He had tethered to a great plane tree.
The wild asses' belly fat and intestines
He boiled in a traveling pot.
From the matchless Brown steed,
He removed the saddle, leaving its back bare.
The prancing great beast,
He shackled and hobbled.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
With his head turned toward Mecca,
Pillowing it on his blue saddlecloth,
Had sunk into a giant sleep.
His snoring split the rocks;
He slept without moving.
His outstretched legs did not draw in,
His closed eyes did not open;
He slept stretched out.
It was Azhybay himself,
His own dark, gazing eyes.
By my Allah's decree, for Azhy
To encounter lion Manas and Bakay,
The time had come.
Wearing out his horse, seeking a hero,
Seeking a hero equal to himself,
In his fervor then,
He had come to the desert.
To the place ordained by God Most High,
He had now arrived.
Seeing a man asleep,
He took his sword in hand,
The bloodthirsty lion bristled,
Intending to cut off his head.
His eyes blazed like a lion's.
‘He is certainly an enemy,’ he said;
His blood-drinking fury seized him indeed,
And Manas readied himself.
Unable to tell whether he was a friend,
Unable to tell whether he was a foe,
As he stood bewildered,
Lion Bakay cried out:
‘Turn your horse's head a moment,
Generous Manas, leopard,
Wait a moment in the place ahead.
Did I not tell you earlier?
Did you not hear earlier?
That tethered brown horse
Seems a beast like Kartküröng.
This man who lies asleep
Seems a man like Azhybay.
Turn your horse's head,
Wait with patience!
At patience's root is yellow gold.
A patient person prospers,
An impatient person falls to ruin.
Do try to heed my words:
Many lions will come to you.
The one asleep before you
Is Azhybay himself.
